content.title: About
content.content: Beef, bacon, cooked is a dish made from beef cuts that have been roasted or fried together with bacon. The result is tender pieces of meat with a distinctive smoky‑salty flavor, high nutritional value, and a rich aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon gives the beef its characteristic aroma through smoking and curing.
Traditionally prepared in the US and UK as part of breakfast or snack plates.
The combination increases iron and zinc content compared with plain beef.
When cooked properly, the meat stays juicy while the bacon stays crisp.
Often served with eggs, potatoes, or vegetable sides.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and bacon together provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The fat content makes the dish calorie‑rich, useful for those with higher energy needs.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Bacon is high in saturated fat, so moderate consumption is advised, especially for people with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Bacon is salty, which can raise blood pressure in sodium‑sensitive individuals.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The dish is calorie‑dense, so portion control is important.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to beef.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as part of breakfast, lunch, or dinner. It is often diced and added to salads, omelets, sandwiches, or potato sides. It can also be incorporated into casseroles and pasta dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

chicken-or-turkey-fricassee-no-sauce-no-.title: Chicken or Turkey Fricassee, No Sauce, No Potatoes, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey fricassee without sauce or potatoes is a traditional Puerto Rican dish that dates back to 1598. The meat is slowly braised in its own juices with aromatic spices such as adobo, oregano, garlic, and onion, resulting in a tender, flavorful dish without the need for additional sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Puerto Rico in 1598 when Spanish colonists adapted European recipes to local ingredients.
Originally made with chicken, turkey later became a popular alternative because of its firmer texture.
The absence of sauce and potatoes makes the dish lighter and lets the spice blend shine.
A typical seasoning includes "pimienton," a dried pepper blend characteristic of Puerto Rican cuisine.
It is often served with rice, beans, or crusty bread to soak up the savory broth.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Without potatoes or sauce, the dish fits well into low‑carb dietary patterns.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: Turkey offers a good amount of iron, while chicken is a solid source of zinc, both important for immune function.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies B6 and B12 vitamins that support nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Low fat when prepared properly
items.content: Braising without excess oil keeps saturated fat levels modest.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Meat must reach an internal temperature of at least 74 °C (165 °F) to eliminate salmonella and other pathogens.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin or respiratory reactions.

items.title: Sodium content in spices
items.content: Traditional adobo seasoning can be salty; those monitoring sodium should adjust the amount used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the chicken or turkey into bite‑size pieces, sear briefly in a little oil until golden, then add chopped onion, garlic, adobo, oregano, and a splash of water or broth. Cover and simmer on low heat for 45–60 minutes until the meat is tender. Serve hot with rice, beans, or bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F) before serving.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-poultry-and-added.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce, Poultry and Added Vegetables (Ready‑to‑Heat)

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce, chicken and added vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat product designed for a quick hot meal. It contains cooked pasta, a smooth cream sauce, pieces of chicken breast and a mix of vegetables (carrot, broccoli, bell pepper). The dish is nutritious and balanced, ready in 3–5 minutes in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is made from dairy and vegetable oils, giving the dish a silky texture and mild flavor.
Chicken breast provides a lean source of protein that is easy to digest and suitable for diet meals.
Vegetables retain most of their vitamins and minerals thanks to a brief heat treatment.
The pasta used is typically durum wheat, which gives a lower glycemic index compared with soft pasta.
The product is packaged in a single‑serve pouch, making storage and transport convenient.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Chicken supplies essential amino acids needed for muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The cream sauce and chicken contain vitamin B6 and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Carrots, broccoli and bell pepper provide beta‑carotene and vitamin C, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Balanced fat profile
items.content: The cream sauce includes both saturated and monounsaturated fats, offering energy and aiding absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Moderate carbohydrate level
items.content: Pasta delivers a steady release of glucose, helping to maintain stable blood sugar.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cream sauce may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑to‑heat meals can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Heat safety
items.content: Insufficient heating may leave the product unsafe; heat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives may be used to extend shelf life, which some sensitive consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the pouch in a microwave (800 W) for 3–4 minutes, stir, then heat an additional 1–2 minutes until piping hot. It can also be warmed in a skillet with a splash of water or broth. Serve as a standalone dish or with a fresh green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0 °C to +4 °C. Shelf life is printed on the package; after opening, consume within 2–3 days. When frozen, the product retains quality for up to 3 months.

rice-white-with-peas-and-carrots-fat-add.title: White Rice with Peas and Carrots, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: White rice with peas and carrots is a ready‑to‑eat dish that combines steamed white rice, green peas, carrots, and a small amount of added vegetable fat. The dish has a mild flavor, pleasant texture, and can be served as a side or a main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of rice, peas, and carrots provides a variety of flavors and nutrients in one meal.
Such mixes are traditionally prepared in Asian cuisines, where rice is often paired with vegetables and a touch of oil.
Adding fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins found in carrots.
The dish is easy to store and reheat, making it popular in cafeterias and home cooking.
White rice supplies a quick source of energy due to its easily digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice is a good source of carbohydrates that are rapidly converted into energy, supporting activity levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice and peas contain B1, B3, and B6 vitamins, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Peas add plant‑based protein, which helps with tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Vitamin A from carrots
items.content: Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, supporting vision.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from peas and carrots promotes healthy gut function and contributes to satiety.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes, including peas.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Added fat increases the calorie count; those watching weight should account for it in their overall diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable patties. It is also convenient for lunch boxes – reheat in a microwave for 1‑2 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. When frozen, it lasts up to 2 months. Before eating, reheat to at least 75 °C.
